subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinothalamic, dorsal column, and corticospinal pathways
vignette: A 40-year-old man suffers a small lesion in the anterior white commissure of his spinal cord.
question: Which sensory modalities are most likely lost as a result of this lesion?

options.text: Vibration and proprioception below the lesion
Fine touch and pressure below the lesion
Motor strength on the ipsilateral side below the lesion
Conscious proprioception and two-point discrimination
Pain and temperature sensation on the contralateral side below the lesion

explanation_correct: The anterior white commissure is where second-order spinothalamic neurons cross after synapsing in the posterior horn. These fibers carry pain and temperature from A-delta and C fibers, so a lesion there produces contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning a few levels below the lesion. Vibration, fine touch, and proprioception travel in the dorsal columns and are unaffected, and motor strength is carried by the separate corticospinal tract. This is the classic pattern of a small central cord lesion such as syringomyelia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Vibration and proprioception are dorsal column modalities that cross in the medulla, not in the anterior white commissure.
explanation_incorrect.B: Fine touch and pressure are carried by the dorsal columns, which are not affected by an anterior white commissure lesion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Motor strength is carried by the corticospinal tract, which crosses in the medulla rather than the anterior white commissure.
explanation_incorrect.D: Conscious proprioception and two-point discrimination are dorsal column functions and remain intact.

educationalObjective: The anterior white commissure carries crossed spinothalamic pain and temperature fibers, so a lesion causes contralateral pain/temperature loss.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinothalamic, dorsal column, and corticospinal pathways
vignette: A medical student traces the pathway of a painful stimulus originating in the right hand as it travels toward the cortex.
question: At which site do second-order spinothalamic neurons decussate?

options.text: In the spinal cord via the anterior white commissure
In the nucleus gracilis of the medulla
At the pyramidal decussation of the caudal medulla
In the VPL nucleus of the thalamus
In the posterior limb of the internal capsule

explanation_correct: First-order spinothalamic neurons enter the spinal cord and synapse in the posterior horn. The second-order neurons then decussate in the anterior white commissure of the cord and ascend contralaterally as the spinothalamic tract, synapsing in the VPL nucleus of the thalamus before projecting to the primary somatosensory cortex. This synapse-then-cross pattern is characteristic of ascending tracts. The nucleus gracilis, pyramidal decussation, and internal capsule belong to other pathways.

explanation_incorrect.B: The nucleus gracilis is the dorsal column relay for the lower limb and is not part of the spinothalamic decussation.
explanation_incorrect.C: The pyramidal decussation is where the descending corticospinal motor tract crosses, not the spinothalamic tract.
explanation_incorrect.D: The VPL thalamus is where third-order spinothalamic neurons synapse, after the crossing has already occurred.
explanation_incorrect.E: The internal capsule carries corticospinal and thalamocortical fibers, not the spinothalamic decussation.

educationalObjective: Spinothalamic second-order neurons cross in the anterior white commissure of the cord, then ascend to VPL and primary somatosensory cortex.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinothalamic, dorsal column, and corticospinal pathways
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has a lesion that destroys the right nucleus cuneatus in the medulla.
question: Which of the following deficits would be expected from this lesion?

options.text: Loss of pain and temperature in the left arm
Loss of vibration and proprioception in the left leg
Loss of vibration, fine touch, and proprioception in the right arm above T6
Spastic weakness of the right arm
Loss of pain and temperature in the right arm

explanation_correct: The nucleus cuneatus is the lateral dorsal column nucleus in the medulla that receives fibers from the upper limb above T6, carrying vibration, fine touch, pressure, and conscious proprioception. Because dorsal column fibers ascend ipsilaterally and synapse in the medulla before crossing, a lesion of the right nucleus cuneatus causes ipsilateral loss of these modalities in the right arm above T6. The fibers cross just above this level as the medial lemniscus, so a lesion of the medial lemniscus would instead cause contralateral loss.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pain and temperature are spinothalamic modalities and are not affected by a lesion of a dorsal column nucleus.
explanation_incorrect.B: The lower limb below T6 is carried in the fasciculus gracilis and nucleus gracilis, not the cuneatus.
explanation_incorrect.D: Spastic weakness would indicate corticospinal tract involvement, not a sensory nucleus lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pain and temperature are carried by the spinothalamic tract and would remain intact.

educationalObjective: A nucleus cuneatus lesion causes ipsilateral loss of vibration, fine touch, and proprioception in the upper limb above T6.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinothalamic, dorsal column, and corticospinal pathways
vignette: A medical student traces a descending corticospinal fiber from the left primary motor cortex to a lower motor neuron supplying the right hand.
question: Which of the following correctly orders the structures this corticospinal fiber passes through?

options.text: Internal capsule to cerebral peduncle to anterior horn to pyramidal decussation to neuromuscular junction
Internal capsule to cerebral peduncle to pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla to lateral corticospinal tract to anterior horn to neuromuscular junction
Cerebral peduncle to internal capsule to medial lemniscus to anterior horn to neuromuscular junction
Internal capsule to pyramidal decussation to cerebral peduncle to dorsal column to neuromuscular junction
Corticospinal fibers descend contralaterally from the cortex without ever decussating

explanation_correct: Upper motor neurons from the primary motor cortex descend ipsilaterally through the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the cerebral peduncle, then decussate at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla. They continue contralaterally as the lateral corticospinal tract and synapse on lower motor neurons in the anterior horn, whose axons exit to the neuromuscular junction. This cross-then-synapse pattern is the reverse of the ascending sensory tracts. The internal capsule is a common site of lacunar strokes.

explanation_incorrect.A: The anterior horn synapse occurs after the pyramidal decussation, not before it.
explanation_incorrect.C: The medial lemniscus is a sensory dorsal column pathway, not part of the corticospinal tract, and the internal capsule is traversed before the cerebral peduncle.
explanation_incorrect.D: The cerebral peduncle is traversed before the pyramidal decussation, and the dorsal column is a sensory pathway unused by descending motor fibers.
explanation_incorrect.E: Corticospinal fibers do decussate at the caudal medulla, so most descend contralaterally after crossing.

educationalObjective: Corticospinal fibers descend ipsilaterally through internal capsule and cerebral peduncle, cross at the caudal medulla, then synapse on anterior horn lower motor neurons.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinothalamic, dorsal column, and corticospinal pathways
vignette: A 58-year-old man has a small lacunar infarct in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of his left thalamus.
question: Which of the following best describes the sensory deficit expected from this lesion?

options.text: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature only
Ipsilateral loss of all sensation below the lesion
Contralateral spastic hemiparesis
Contralateral loss of pain, temperature, vibration, and fine touch from the body
Ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception with preserved pain sensation

explanation_correct: The VPL nucleus of the thalamus is the relay station for both the spinothalamic and the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathways from the body, and third-order neurons from VPL project to the primary somatosensory cortex. Because both ascending sensory systems have already decussated before reaching VPL, a left VPL lesion produces contralateral right-sided loss of pain, temperature, vibration, fine touch, and proprioception. Sensation from the face relays through VPM rather than VPL and would be spared.

explanation_incorrect.A: VPL receives both pain and temperature and dorsal column modalities, not pain and temperature alone.
explanation_incorrect.B: The deficit is contralateral, not ipsilateral, because both sensory pathways have crossed before reaching the thalamus.
explanation_incorrect.C: Spastic hemiparesis indicates corticospinal tract damage, not a sensory thalamic nucleus lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: An ipsilateral dorsal-column-only pattern occurs with a cord lesion before the medullary crossing, not with a VPL thalamic lesion.

educationalObjective: VPL thalamus relays all body sensory modalities after they have crossed, so a lesion causes contralateral loss of pain, temperature, vibration, and touch.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Spinothalamic, dorsal column, and corticospinal pathways
vignette: A 50-year-old woman has a small infarct in the right medulla involving the medial lemniscus but sparing the spinothalamic tract.
question: Which sensory findings would most likely be present?

options.text: Loss of pain and temperature in the left arm and leg
Loss of pain and temperature in the right arm and leg
Loss of vibration and proprioception in the right arm and leg
Loss of vibration and proprioception only in the left leg
Loss of vibration, fine touch, and proprioception in the left arm and leg with preserved pain and temperature

explanation_correct: The medial lemniscus is the crossed continuation of the dorsal columns, formed after second-order neurons decussate in the medulla. A lesion of the right medial lemniscus therefore causes contralateral left-sided loss of vibration, fine touch, pressure, and proprioception in both the arm and leg, since the fibers are already crossed and reorganized at this level. Because the spinothalamic tract is spared, pain and temperature remain intact. This contrasts with a dorsal column lesion before the medulla, which causes ipsilateral loss below the lesion.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pain and temperature are spinothalamic modalities and are spared here; the medial lemniscus carries dorsal column modalities.
explanation_incorrect.B: Pain and temperature are unaffected, and a right medullary lesion would affect the contralateral left body.
explanation_incorrect.C: After the medulla, dorsal column fibers are crossed, so the deficit would be contralateral left, not ipsilateral right.
explanation_incorrect.D: The medial lemniscus carries both arm cuneate and leg gracile fibers after the crossing, not the leg alone.

educationalObjective: A medullary medial lemniscus lesion causes contralateral loss of vibration, proprioception, and fine touch with sparing of pain and temperature.
